newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia to have growth if it sticks to reforms.
newsitem.headline: Croatia to have growth if it sticks to reforms.

text.p: EBRD, the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, foresees a steady economic growth in Croatia in 1996 and next few years, provided the country adhers to reforms initiated a few years ago, a bank's deputy chief economist Ricardo Lago said on Monday.
"This year (Croatia) can attain a growth rate of probably over five percent," Lago told journalists after presenting the EBRD's 1996 transition report.

He said Croatia had a potential to keep up the strong trend and boost growth rates. But like many other reform countries, he warned it still had to undertake deeper structural reforms in corporate and financial sectors.
While ranking it among the most advanced reformers of the former communist countries, Lago said Croatia must press on with privatisation and consolidation of all legal and market institutions.
"We should not be so naive to trivialise challenges that lie ahead and assume growth can be taken for granted," he said.
However, among encouraging factors for the future, he outlined Croatia's record of achieving and maintaining price and exchange rate stability over the past three years.
The EBRD estimates Croatia's average inflation at 3.5 percent this year, in line with official forecasts and up from 1.6 percent in 1995.
Its ability to resume growth in 1994 after recovering quickly from the 1991-95 war in former Yugoslavia was also viewed as very positive.

Croatia is among the bank's bigger borrowers with 350 ecus so far, or five percent of its investment portfolio, although its 4.8 million inhabittants represent a little more than one percent of the total population of the region it supports.
Lago said the EBRD would continue to provide it with financing, particularly to enable the recovery of the tourist sector he described as "one of the pillars of growth".

After granting Croatia 50 million German marks to refurbish coastal hotels last summer, the bank on Monday signed another 105 million marks loan for environmental projects in the tourist region of Dalmatia.
"As soon as tourism picks up, the outlook can be for rates between five and seven percent -- as long as a stable macroeconomic environment is preserved," he said.
